paper_a.title: A motivated exposition of the proof of Tverberg's theorem

metadata.description: Paper A is a self-contained motivated exposition of Tverberg's theorem (any (d+1)(r-1)+1 points in R^d admit an r-partition with intersecting convex hulls), proved via lifting and the Colorful Caratheodory theorem. Paper B (Perles-Sigron) treats Tverberg as a cited classical result and studies the Tverberg-Reay relaxation T(d,r,k) in which only every k of the r convex hulls need to share a point; it proves Reay's conjecture T(d,r,k)=T(d,r) in two regimes (k>=floor((d+3)/2) and d<rk/(r-k)-1) and works out the boundary cases T(3,4,2)=T(5,3,2)=13. The alignment is therefore an EXT relationship: paper A states/proves the core Tverberg statement that paper B generalizes by varying the intersection pattern.

matches.explanation: Both nodes state the classical Tverberg theorem: any (d+1)(r-1)+1 points in R^d can be partitioned into r groups whose convex hulls share a common point. Paper A states it as its main result (origin=paper) and proves it; paper B cites it as the foundational classical result (origin=external, attributed to Tverberg 1966) that defines the baseline Tverberg number T(d,r) it then varies. The fact that A's main contribution appears as B's external prior work is the canonical signal for an EXT relationship.

Both state Radon's theorem: any d+2 points in R^d split into two groups with intersecting convex hulls. Paper A treats it as a paper-origin warm-up that motivates and is later subsumed by Tverberg (cf. RP425.2 noting r=2). Paper B cites it only externally as classical background. Same statement, paper-origin in A vs cited-external in B.

Paper A explicitly defines the convex hull of a finite set as the set of convex combinations. Paper B uses convex hulls throughout (conv C, conv a(N_j)) but never extracts a separate definition node; conv is treated as a primitive of standard convex geometry. The absence is one of granularity rather than substance: paper A is expository and defines its objects from scratch, while paper B is a research paper that assumes them. No suitable B-side counterpart exists, so the match is none.

Paper B encodes Tverberg's theorem partially through the Tverberg number definition T(d,r)=(d+1)(r-1)+1, which packages the threshold of A's TP425.2 as a numerical invariant whose existence is exactly Tverberg's theorem. The two play the same conceptual role -- the number whose finiteness is guaranteed by Tverberg -- but B reorganizes the statement as a function-valued definition (so it can then be relaxed to T(d,r,k)).

Paper B's central conceptual move is to introduce the Tverberg-Reay number T(d,r,k) (DP408.2) and the corresponding determination problem (ProbP408.1), where only every k of the r convex hulls need to intersect. This is the explicit generalization of paper A's Tverberg statement (k=r is exactly Tverberg). The match is analogous because B's object is a strict superset -- T(d,r,r) recovers TP425.2 -- and B is asking the new question that A's theorem answers only at the endpoint.

Paper A's full proof of Tverberg via the Sarkaria/Barany lifting + Colorful Caratheodory machinery has no analogue in paper B. Paper B never reproves Tverberg (it cites it as TP408.1) and uses an entirely different toolkit -- positive bases of d-simplex rays, support indices I(C), and weight-counting arguments -- to attack the Reay variant. The proof technique of A is not what B extends; B extends the statement and develops new machinery to handle weaker intersection demands.

Paper A's standalone proof of Radon (lift to R^{d+1}, take a linear dependence, partition by sign) has no counterpart in paper B. Paper B never reproves Radon; it only cites it. The expository inclusion of Radon-as-stepping-stone is specific to A's didactic goal.

Barany's Colorful Caratheodory theorem is the workhorse external lemma in paper A. Paper B does not invoke it -- its arguments use Helly's theorem (TP408.3) and direct positive-basis combinatorics instead. The non-appearance is structurally informative: B's generalization route bypasses A's main external tool entirely, indicating that EXT here is at the statement level, not via a generalized Colorful Caratheodory.

Helly's theorem is invoked by paper B to handle the trivial regime k>=d+1 of T(d,r,k). It plays no role in paper A. Even though TP408.3 is origin=external in B, it is listed as a none entry because its presence in B and absence in A is itself a marker of how B's generalization path differs methodologically from A.

Reay's conjecture T(d,r,k)=T(d,r) for all 2<=k<=r is the central organizing question of paper B and is what motivates each of B's main theorems (TP408.4-7 are listed as `specializes` of CnjP408.1). Paper A predates the question by stating only the k=r (Tverberg) case. This is the cleanest expression of the EXT direction at the question-level: B asks a strictly more general question than A answers.

Main theorem of paper B: T(d,r,floor((d+3)/2))=(d+1)(r-1)+1 for all r>=floor((d+3)/2). This is a paper-original generalization of Tverberg in the sense that it shows the Tverberg threshold suffices already for the much weaker k-wise intersection demand once k>=floor((d+3)/2). No analogue in A.

T(3,4,2)=13: a small-case witness that Reay's conjecture holds at d=3, r=4, k=2. Paper-original to B; absent from A. Interesting because (3,4,2) lies in a regime not covered by either of B's general theorems and requires a case-by-case enumeration of 18 good 4-partitions plus an explicit perturbation argument.

Second main theorem of B: for 2<=k<r and d<rk/(r-k)-1, T(d,r,k)=(d+1)(r-1)+1. This is a complementary regime to TP408.4, established by induction on r combined with a double-counting weight argument. Paper A has no analogue.

T(5,3,2)=13: the boundary case d+1=rk/(r-k), which TP408.6 just misses. Resolved by enumerating 120 good 3-partitions and killing them in three explicit perturbation steps. Paper-original to B; not relevant to A.

Positive basis P={p_0,...,p_d} (vertices of a d-simplex centered at the origin, sum to zero, every d linearly independent), together with the rays R_i=R_{>0} p_i. This is the foundational construction of paper B -- all subsequent definitions (support, I(C), lower/higher) are anchored to it. Paper A has no positive-basis machinery; its Tverberg proof goes through the Sarkaria lift instead.
Non-negative representation x = sum xi_i p_i with min xi_i = 0 and its support supp x. Specific to paper B's positive-basis framework; absent from paper A.
Index set I(C) = {i : C meets R_i} and ray union R(I). Combinatorial bookkeeping used pervasively in paper B's arguments; no counterpart in paper A.
Lower/higher comparison of points on a single ray R_i. The ordering structure on rays is a B-only ingredient and drives the separation arguments PrP408.4, PrP408.5.
Highest/middle/lowest points p_{i,1}, p_{i,2}, p_{i,3} on each ray, used in the (3,4,2) case analysis. Specific to that section of B; not present in A.
(M,X)-selection: a transversal of one point per ray indexed by M. Used to define general position in paper B; no counterpart in paper A.
General position of X in B's setup (intersections of affine hulls of selections behave generically). A B-only definition serving as a working hypothesis for TP408.6 and its proof.
Common rays I(J) = intersection of I(C_j) over j in J. Combinatorial primitive for B's lower-bound machinery on the weight function; not in A.
Weight function W counting how many of k chosen parts meet a ray with multiplicity. Drives the double-counting bound k*C(r,k) <= (d+1)*C(r-1,k) at the core of TP408.6. B-specific.

Bad/good partition: bad if some two parts have disjoint convex hulls, good otherwise. Specific terminology of B's perturbation arguments; A does not need this distinction since A is establishing existence (k=r) rather than ruling out (k=2).
Separating hyperplane H_{k,l} = aff(R_k union R_l) used in the (3,4,2) perturbation argument. B-specific.
Existence and uniqueness of the non-negative representation x = sum xi_i p_i. A foundational lemma for B's positive-basis framework; A uses no analogous statement.
Support containment supp x subset of I(C) when x is in conv C. Bookkeeping result internal to B.
Restriction to common rays: x in conv C reduces to conv(C cap R(supp x)). Internal lemma of B's geometric machinery.

Disjointness via lower/higher: if for each i in I, every C-point on R_i is lower than every C'-point, then conv C and conv C' are disjoint. The basic separation lemma underpinning all of B's lower-bound proofs; no analogue in A.

Key empty-intersection criterion (the technical heart of TP408.4): packages PrP408.2-4 into a usable hypothesis-based criterion for n>=2 parts to have empty intersection of convex hulls. Used directly in PP408.6, PP408.10, PrP408.14. B-internal.
Bound |I(C_1) cap I(C_2) \ U| <= floor((d-1)/2). A counting lemma feeding the proof of TP408.4. B-internal.
Stability of badness under small perturbations. A general principle used in B's perturbation strategy for TP408.5 and TP408.7; not relevant to A.
If |I(C_i)|<3 for some part in a 4-partition (d=3 setting), the partition is bad. Step in B's (3,4,2) case analysis.
Two-side lower-comparison forces disjoint hulls in the (3,4,2) setting. B-specific.
Lowest/middle/highest distribution across the four parts of a good (3,4)-partition. Combinatorial reduction in B's enumeration of the 18 good 4-partitions.
Common rays govern intersections of convex hulls. Lower-bound machinery in B's weight argument.
Mutual rays bound, base case: |I(J)|<k with each common ray hit exactly once forces empty intersection. Stepping stone to PrP408.13.
Generalized mutual rays bound: m<k-t implies empty intersection. Provides the lower bound EP408.2 used in TP408.6.
Characterization of good (5,3,2)-partitions via the lower/higher pattern across pairs. Reduction in the (5,3,2) proof of TP408.7.
Hyperplane separating C_1 from C_2 in the (5,3,2) construction. B-specific separation lemma.
Perturbation that strictly separates conv C_1 from conv C_2 in the (5,3,2) setting. Used in PP408.9 to dispose of remaining good partitions.
The non-negative representation formula x = sum xi_i p_i with min xi_i=0. Internal to B's framework.
Lower bound sum_i W >= k. Counting inequality in TP408.6.
Upper bound sum_J W <= C(r-1,k) per ray. Counting inequality in TP408.6.
Combined bound k*C(r,k) <= (d+1)*C(r-1,k), equivalent to d >= rk/(r-k)-1. Decisive inequality of TP408.6's proof.
Two-set partition equality used in the proof of Radon. Local algebraic identity in A's exposition; no counterpart in B which avoids this proof path entirely.
Lifted-vector reformulation p_i^+ = (p_i,1) in R^{d+1} converting the two equalities into a single equation. The Sarkaria lift is the heart of A's machinery and absent in B.
Three-set partition equality (r=3 case) in A's proof of Tverberg. Algebraic prelude to the auxiliary vectors; no counterpart in B.
Auxiliary vectors phi_{j,i} in R^{2d+2} packaging the two equalities into one. Specific to A's Sarkaria-style argument.
Single-equation form (2) used to invoke Colorful Caratheodory. A-specific.

All of these are 'proofs that show some Tverberg-type partition exists / fails to exist for a given (d,r,k)'. PP425.2 establishes the original Tverberg statement (k=r) via Colorful Caratheodory. PP408.6-9 establish lower-bound / upper-bound parts of T(d,r,k)=T(d,r) in the Reay relaxation, using positive-basis machinery and weight rebalancing. They share a common goal -- decide whether (d+1)(r-1)+1 points always admit the desired partition pattern -- but employ disjoint techniques. Listed as a many-to-many composite to expose the conceptual sibling-relationship between A's Tverberg proof and B's family of proofs of Tverberg-Reay variants.

Open problem: does T(d,r,k)<T(d,r) for some (d,r,k) with 2<=k<r and d large (e.g., is T(d,3,2)<2d+3 for d>=6)? This is the natural counter-direction to Reay's conjecture and is paper-original to B as a posed question. Paper A does not engage with the variant T(d,r,k) at all and so has no analogue.

Proofs of B's positive-basis lemmas PrP408.1, PrP408.3, PrP408.4, PrP408.5, PrP408.6 respectively. None correspond to anything in A: A does not develop a positive-basis framework, so the entire proof family is B-only machinery serving the Reay-direction generalization.

Proofs supporting B's (3,4,2)=13 result: PP408.10 (small |I(C_i)| forces bad), PP408.11 (lowest/middle/highest distribution), PP408.12 (perturbation preserves badness). All three are case-specific perturbation/combinatorial arguments with no analogue in A's exposition of the original Tverberg theorem.

Proofs of the 'common-rays govern intersection' chain (PrP408.11), the mutual-rays base case (PrP408.12), and its m<k-t generalization (PrP408.13) -- the lower-bound side of the weight argument inside TP408.6. B-internal machinery that has no counterpart in A.

Proofs of the (5,3,2) lemmas: PrP408.14 (good-partition characterization) and PrP408.16 (perturbation-based separation of conv C_1 from conv C_2). Specific to B's perturbation argument for TP408.7; not present in A.
